R_H1.passageTitle: Designing Furniture for Homes That Must Do More

passages.label: A
passages.text: A multinational furniture company may have a reputation for selling the same products in many places. Yet a room used for meals in one home may have to hold a bed, a desk and a chair in another. To study domestic routines, IKEA researchers visit homes and see where families put things and what they move during the day. Their observations have an influence on which features people see as a selling point, and it is easy to confuse a room’s size with the amount of space actually available for daily use.

passages.label: B
passages.text: One project began with visits and other research in Hong Kong and Japan, where a substantial number of people live in small urban homes. IKEA and the design company Ori used that evidence to develop ROGNAN, a robotic furniture system. With a touchpad, residents could move a large unit and change the same area from a bedroom into a wardrobe, workplace or living room. The companies said the system could create about eight extra square metres of usable space. Its main selling point was not a new room, but several uses for one room.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Another IKEA team experimented with simpler moving parts, and it tested a bed that folded against a wall and became a desk, a wardrobe that rolled aside, and storage that remained reachable in each arrangement. The idea was to let one room support work, learning and sleep at different times. Designers had to ensure that moving a unit did not block a door or make daily objects difficult to reach, and a clever transformation would offer little convenience if residents needed to empty every shelf before using it.

passages.label: D
passages.text: The RÅVAROR collection explored the same problem without robotic equipment. IKEA asked designers to imagine all the belongings in a twelve-square-metre home. The resulting group included a daybed, tables, storage boxes, textiles, lighting and a small kitchen. Several pieces had castors, so a resident could move them and make room for another activity. Bags and boxes were sized to travel with the furniture, and these practical features suited people who expected to move again and could not fit the same large piece into every new home.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Researchers use these observations to form hypotheses about shared space, and designers can experiment with modular fittings that let residents remove a component, continue using the same surface for meals and work, or increase the room left clear for other activities. To ensure a change works at scale, a supplier needs consistent measurements and evidence of what happens when pieces are moved repeatedly. In a relatively small home, convenience depends on who needs space and when, so prototypes can also be assessed against competing demands within the same household.

passages.label: F
passages.text: Before manufacturers produce a piece of furniture, they can investigate the dimensions of the places where a consumer might use it. A resident can purchase one adjustable surface for otherwise incompatible activities, including dining and completing office assignments in limited space. Volume affects the cost of storing finished goods, while production costs also include labour and transport across the supply chain. Compact packaging can require precise assembly instructions and reduce abrasion to exposed surfaces in transit. Where a design meets those conditions, the retailer can consider whether it will earn a profit and suit the space customers actually have.

R_H2.passageTitle: How IKEA Gives Used Furniture Another Chance

passages.label: A
passages.text: A multinational retailer can make it easier for a piece of furniture to continue in use after its first owner no longer needs it. IKEA’s Buyback and Resell service begins online, where the owner provides details to receive an estimate, and this step saves time, but an estimate is not a discount on a new item or a promise to buy the old one. Employees examine the item at the store and can refuse it if its condition falls outside the scheme, which excludes products that cannot be accepted safely.

passages.label: B
passages.text: At the store, staff compare the item with its online description and check its identity, age, condition and functionality. Current United States guidance says an eligible product must be clean, fully assembled and functional. If the item meets the rules, the store provides an IKEA voucher, and the item can then appear in an As-Is area or on a local secondhand page. The clear sequence gives the customer a practical route from estimate to inspection and possible acceptance.

passages.label: C
passages.text: The service operated in 28 markets run by Ingka Group in the 2024 financial year. More than 260,000 customers returned 495,000 pieces of furniture, and the service grew by 15 per cent from the previous year. During the Buyback Friday campaign, almost 55,000 products came back for resale, and the campaign was presented as a secondhand alternative to a shopping period known for heavy buying. These totals show activity at a large scale, but they do not ensure that every item sold immediately or that every returned product avoided disposal.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Repair offers a related way to keep furniture in service. In the same financial year, IKEA distributed 24.6 million assembly parts, supplied small parts free of charge to approximately 2.2 million customers, and provided 190,884 larger pieces including wardrobe fronts, sofa cushions and bed slats. A replacement screw or component may restore the usefulness of a product without requiring the customer to replace it. The environmental value depends on whether the repair actually extends use and avoids additional material consumption, and a record of replacement parts and reassembly allows staff to distinguish warehouse, inspection and distribution costs when assessing whether reuse is efficient.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Design affects what the service can do. If a supplier gives clear details about materials, workers can remove or replace a damaged part more easily. Such choices may increase the time that a product remains usable, and this is relevant to a company’s reputation as well as to material consumption. Inflation can affect what a buyer is willing to pay for new or used furniture, while the convenience of a nearby outlet may affect what an owner does with it. Keeping useful materials in service may slow the rate at which production exhausts certain resources.

passages.label: F
passages.text: An outlet receiving used goods has to investigate wear and record how each item entered the scheme. A consumer may ask about the cost of transport and what it would cost to purchase a new item. Inspection and repair involve labour, yet the work may let the retailer rely less on new items that a supply chain has to produce, import or move overseas. To work out whether the service earns a profit, the company can compare those costs with sales and with the different production costs of making replacements.

R_H3.passageTitle: Slow Food Protects Local Flavour in a Changing Italy

passages.label: A
passages.text: Travel, retail and changes in consumption have made many foods easier to buy in Italy, and a multinational company can put a standard product in many stores, while a small domestic supplier may make only a limited quantity of a local speciality. The convenience of a larger shop can have an influence on which foods become dominant. During inflation, a rise in price may also lead families to change what they buy. Slow Food’s projects ask how people who still want regional products can continue to find them. The organisation’s approach connects food consumption to the ecological conditions and specialised knowledge needed to sustain production.

passages.label: B
passages.text: One Slow Food programme is called the Presidia, and it supports small producers who protect traditional products, landscapes and methods, and a Presidium may bring farmers together, help them agree on production rules, improve quality and explain a product's story to customers. The aim is to help a regional speciality survive as real work rather than as a museum object. Direct sales, markets, restaurants and partnerships with cooks can give producers a steadier path to buyers.

passages.label: C
passages.text: Presidia also connect food with place, and a cheese depends on animal breeds, pasture and ageing skills, and a bean may suit one valley's soil and climate. If these links disappear, copying the name elsewhere does not preserve the same culture. Training and exchanges allow producers to continue sharing knowledge with younger workers. Clear production rules can remove some uncertainty about how a food was made and ensure that buyers can distinguish a protected product from an imitation.

passages.label: D
passages.text: Education is another part of the movement. Italy's Orto in Condotta network creates school gardens with students, teachers, parents, grandparents and local authorities. Over a three-year cycle, children explore their senses, the environment, food production and regional culture, and a garden makes the influence of season and soil visible, and it also shows that food does not begin on a supermarket shelf. Schools can use a relatively small plot to connect lessons with planting, tasting and shared responsibility.

passages.label: E
passages.text: Protecting a speciality requires a distinction between increasing demand and increasing production, because a limited supply may be part of what gives a product its market reputation. Certification and promotion can help ensure that buyers understand how producers work, although higher prices or travel costs can still exclude households. A relatively small rise in demand may sustain a local supplier, whereas a sudden increase could put pressure on ingredients and methods that take time to reproduce.

passages.label: F
passages.text: Local producers have to consider the cost of labour, fuel and transport, as well as how they produce food in a particular place. A consumer may purchase seasonal goods from a nearby supply chain, while a larger shop can import food or help businesses export it. The production costs of a small batch may prevent a local business from making a profit if prices are too low. A community that wants long-term prosperity therefore has to consider how more sales would affect both the producers and the practices people hope to preserve.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why can food from a large company become more common than a local speciality?
options: Local foods are always cheaper when prices rise.
Every large company depends on one valley for ingredients.
People become unable to buy all kinds of food as soon as they travel.
A standard product can reach many convenient shops, while local suppliers may make less.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What is a way a Presidium can help a speciality remain part of everyday work?
options: Bring producers together and help them reach people who will buy what they make.
Move the remaining products into a museum and stop selling them.
Replace different local methods with one standard rule for all products in Italy.
Help only customers who are already buying from the largest stores.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: A producer elsewhere uses a local cheese's name. Why does that alone fail to preserve the food described?
options: Only the label matters if the cheese reaches enough stores.
The food also depends on local animals, land and skills that a name cannot transfer.
The same animals and pasture exist wherever it is sold.
A copied name automatically establishes who followed the production rules.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: What do the school gardens let children understand first-hand?
options: Why a shop can stock all ingredients in every season
How to tell that students can only learn about farming from a supermarket
How the land and time of year affect the food people grow
Why food production must start in a shop rather than a school plot

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How do the programme's rules and activities for younger people support related goals in different ways?
options: Both let customers determine every ingredient without talking to a producer.
Both are used mainly to increase the size of every harvest.
The garden writes rules for a product, and the production rules tell pupils the length of all terms.
Rules can help buyers recognise how a product was made, while a garden gives pupils their own experience of growing food.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Why could a sudden increase in demand have a different effect from a modest one?
options: A small increase can help a producer keep working, while a fast surge may strain supplies and methods that take time.
A short surge guarantees enough ingredients for everyone.
Small and large increases have identical effects as long as a product's name stays the same.
Any rise makes it necessary to stop producing the foods immediately.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which is one limit to what certification and promotion can do?
options: They provide a way to relate the name to how a product was made.
They show buyers some things about the producers.
Some people may still face prices or travel costs they cannot afford.
They remove all distance and price differences among buyers.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: How might seeking the lowest price affect the aim of keeping a speciality available?
options: It makes a higher volume sufficient even when production costs are not covered.
If a price does not cover small-batch costs, the local business may become unable to continue.
Every product with a lower price is easier to make without changing a method.
Replacing producers with lower-cost suppliers preserves the same local knowledge.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which approach would help a town attract buyers while keeping the qualities that make a product local?
options: Stop selling to anyone outside town, since buyers have no role in keeping work viable.
Sell all products under a shared name regardless of how they were made.
Aim for a sudden increase in production without checking available materials.
Give producers reliable ways to sell and consider how extra demand affects the methods and materials they use.

questions.instruction: Choose ONE answer, A–D, for each question.
questions.prompt: Which idea ties the examples and the final argument together?
options: A speciality can remain part of local life when people pass on the knowledge and producers can earn enough without losing what makes it distinctive.
The best way to keep a product local is to make it in as many places as possible without checking its methods.
Learning about food makes marketing, costs and working conditions irrelevant.
A familiar product name is sufficient evidence of local production in every shop.
